# A New Snack Line for a New Market: Recommended Product Strategy

**Prepared for discussion at the management meeting — Revision 1**

*Preparation note: this draft follows the same method as the regional entry paper — one framing decision surfaced early, candidates scored openly, and the working sheet available to anyone who wants it. Input so far from R&D (formulation feasibility), supply chain (co-packing), and two informal conversations: a former category manager at a Mexican convenience chain, and a Guadalajara co-packer who has quoted us on an indicative basis. Where the group has not converged, it is marked. Nothing here is committed. The three decisions in §1 and §2 are the ones worth an hour of leadership attention; the rest can be redirected later at low cost.*

---

## 1. Three framing decisions, before anything else

The brief contains an ambiguity that is worth naming rather than working around. "A new product line tailored to local tastes" can mean two quite different businesses:

- **Mandate A — Flavour localisation.** Take our existing platforms (extrusion, baking, coating) and re-season them for local palates. Fast, cheap, low technical risk. Also: the single most copyable thing in this industry. A dominant incumbent can match a flavour in one quarter.
- **Mandate B — Occasion creation.** Build a product around an eating *behaviour* the local market already has but that no packaged product serves well. Slower, more technically awkward, considerably harder to copy — because the copy has to reproduce a format and a route to market, not a seasoning drum.

Our recommendation is **B carried on A's back**: a line where two or three familiar-format SKUs earn distribution and pay the freight, and two or three genuinely new-to-shelf items do the brand work and hold the margin. A pure-A line will sell and then quietly disappear. A pure-B line will be admired and never listed.

**Third decision, less glamorous and more consequential: make or import.** Exporting from our existing plants preserves control and is the obvious first instinct. It also imports our cost base, our currency, and our lead times into a market that punishes all three. Our view is **import for the pilot, co-pack locally from month nine**, and we have modelled it that way in §7.

**Guidance requested.** If the leadership team's actual priority is near-term volume rather than building a defensible position, say so plainly before Stage 1 spend — the line composition inverts, the concepts in §5 that are marked *high-variance* come out, and the budget in §8 halves. We would rather hear that now than infer it from the reception of this paper.

---

## 2. Market selection — candidates scored

The brief specifies "a target international market" without naming one. Rather than assume, we scored six. Weights were agreed with commercial and R&D before scoring.

| Criterion | Weight | **Mexico** | Indonesia | Nigeria | Saudi/Gulf | Vietnam | Poland/CEE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Snacking frequency & per-capita savoury snack spend | 20% | 5 | 5 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3 |
| Distinctiveness of local flavour system (i.e. how much a *tailored* line is actually worth) | 15% | 5 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 2 |
| Structural white space (regulatory, occasion, or format gap a newcomer can occupy) | 20% | 5 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| Route-to-market accessibility for a non-incumbent | 15% | 2 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| Local ingredient & co-packing depth | 10% | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 5 |
| Willingness to pay above mainstream price | 10% | 3 | 2 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 3 |
| Cheap testing infrastructure (social commerce, quick-commerce, modern trade density) | 10% | 4 | 5 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 3 |
| **Weighted total** | | **4.20** | **3.75** | **2.80** | **3.60** | **3.35** | **3.20** |

**Recommendation: Mexico.**

Not because it is easy — on route-to-market it is the *worst* of the six, and that is a real cost, addressed in §6. But it is the only candidate where a specific, dateable, structural opening exists that the incumbents are structurally slow to fill. That opening is §4, and it is the reason this paper exists in its current form.

**Runners-up, one line each:**

- **Indonesia** — the strongest pure snacking market on the list and a genuinely exciting flavour landscape (sambal, rendang, seaweed, the whole *kerupuk* architecture). It loses on white space: the local field is crowded, fast, and very good at exactly this. **Kept warm as market two, from Year 3, with several §5 concepts translatable.**
- **Saudi/Gulf** — best price ceiling, weakest local flavour distinctiveness for a *tailored* line, and largely served by imports already.
- **Vietnam** — attractive and rising; we would not close the door, but the premium ceiling is not yet where the concepts in §5 need it.
- **Nigeria** — enormous latent demand, and route-to-market and FX repatriation are not problems we should take on with a first international line.
- **Poland/CEE** — lowest ambiguity, lowest reward; a flavour-extension market, not a new-line market.

---

## 3. Competitive map — Mexico

Mexico's savoury snack category is among the most concentrated in the world. Sabritas (PepsiCo) is generally put in the region of three-quarters of the salty snack market, with Barcel (Grupo Bimbo) the principal challenger. Any plan that involves meeting either of them head-on in their own format, at their own price, on their own shelf, is not a plan.

| Incumbent | What they own | Approx. shelf price band | Where they are slow, and our wedge |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sabritas (PepsiCo)** | Direct store delivery to hundreds of thousands of outlets; the impulse shelf itself | MXN 15–45 | Portfolio scale makes reformulation to a *seal-free* profile commercially awkward — it would cannibalise their own core. We start clean. |
| **Barcel — Takis, Chips, Runners** | Extreme-flavour teen/young adult; the most copy-fast operator in the market | MXN 15–40 | They win on intensity. We do not out-intense them. We win on *format novelty* and on adult/parent-facing credibility they have deliberately not built. |
| **Grupo Bimbo / Ricolino (sweet & confection)** | Lonchera, bakery, tamarind & chamoy confectionery | MXN 10–35 | Sweet-side strength, thin on savoury-nutritious. Our seed/legume tier does not meet them. |
| **Street vendors — esquites, fruta con chile, tostilocos carts** | The *occasion*. Fresh, made-to-order, unbeatable on flavour authenticity | MXN 25–70 | They cannot travel, cannot be stocked, cannot be bought at 9pm in an OXXO. This is the gap our headline concept walks into. |
| **Better-for-you challengers** (bean/plantain/amaranth crisps, regional artisan) | Credibility with urban ABC+ shoppers | MXN 45–90 | Fragmented, sub-scale, weak on flavour excitement — usually "healthy first, tasty second." We invert the order. |
| **US imports (Costco/Sam's/City Market)** | Premium novelty | MXN 90–200 | Rarely localised beyond a Spanish sticker. Poor value-to-substance. |

**Honest reading.** There is no wedge available in "a better potato chip." There is a real one at the intersection of *street-food occasion + packaged convenience + a nutrition profile that clears the regulatory bar*. Nobody at scale is standing there, and the reason is in the next section.

---

## 4. The structural opening — and why incumbents are slow to take it

Mexico's front-of-pack warning system (NOM-051, phased from 2020) puts black octagonal **EXCESO DE…** seals on products above thresholds for calories, sugars, saturated fat, trans fat and sodium, plus advisory legends for sweeteners and caffeine. Two downstream consequences matter more than the seals themselves:

1. **A product carrying any seal cannot use characters, mascots, celebrities or child-directed animation on pack or in advertising.**
2. **School-adjacent and in-school sale of seal-bearing products has been progressively restricted, with a substantially tightened regime from 2025.**

*All thresholds and dates in this section to be confirmed in writing by Mexican regulatory counsel at Stage 0 — indicative figures only, from our own reading:*

| Seal | Threshold (solid foods, approx.) | Difficulty for a dry snack |
|---|---|---|
| Exceso calorías | ≥275 kcal / 100 g | **Very hard** — a fried chip runs ~500 kcal/100 g |
| Exceso sodio | ≥1 mg sodium per kcal (or ≥300 mg/100 g on low-energy items) | **Hard** — the binding constraint on savoury |
